title: The Mystical Neelachakra and the Patitapabana Flag of Shree Jagannath Temple

translations.or: ପୁରୀ ଶ୍ରୀମନ୍ଦିରର ୨୧୪ ଫୁଟ ଉଚ୍ଚ ଶିଖରରେ ଅଷ୍ଟଧାତୁ ନିର୍ମିତ ନୀଳଚକ୍ର ଶୋଭାପାଉଛି। ପ୍ରତ୍ୟେକ ଦିନ ଅପରାହ୍ଣରେ ନିର୍ଭୀକ ଚୁନରା ସେବକମାନେ କୌଣସି ଦଉଡ଼ିର ସାହାଯ୍ୟ ବିନା ମନ୍ଦିର ଚୂଡ଼ାକୁ ଚଢ଼ି ପତିତପାବନ ବାନା ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତନ କରନ୍ତି।
translations.hi: पुरी श्री जगन्नाथ मंदिर के 214 फीट ऊँचे शिखर पर अष्टधातु से निर्मित नीलचक्र सुशोभित है। प्रतिदिन दोपहर में निडर चुनरा सेवक बिना किसी रस्सी के शिखर पर चढ़कर पतितपावन ध्वज बदलते हैं।

storyText: High above the sacred Shreemandira of Puri, soaring 214 feet into the sky, rests the divine Neelachakra. Cast from Ashtadhatu—an eight-metal alloy of iron, copper, zinc, gold, silver, lead, tin, and mercury—it weighs over two tonnes and has defied the abrasive salty sea winds of the Bay of Bengal for centuries. Every afternoon between 4:30 and 5:30 PM, visitors gather along the Bada Danda to witness one of the most awe-inspiring rituals on earth: a hereditary Chunara servitor, barefoot and gripping the vertical stone carvings without safety ropes, scales the curvilinear spire carrying sacred cloth flags tied around his waist. He removes the previous day’s flag and unfurls the triangular Patitapabana Dhwaja, which famously flutters in defiance of prevailing wind currents, offering visual benediction to all who cannot enter the sanctum.

storyText: Long before the Revolt of 1857, the densely forested ridges of Barunei Hill in Khordha bore witness to the fierce Paika Bidroha—India’s first organized armed rebellion against British East India Company hegemony. Led by Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhara Mohapatra, the hereditary military commander of the Khordha kingdom, the peasant militia (Paikas) took up traditional battle-axes (Khanda), spears, and matchlocks. The catalyst was ruthless colonial agrarian policies that stripped native martial clans of their rent-free Barabati lands and devalued local cowrie currency. Joined by the tribal Kondhs of Ghumusar and Banapur, the Paikas burned British police stations, seized colonial treasuries, and drove the English garrison out of Puri. For seven years, the Paika warriors waged jungle guerrilla warfare from subterranean caves in Barunei, engraving their defiance indelibly into Odishan freedom lore.

storyText: Strategically positioned at the fork of the mighty Mahanadi and Kathajodi rivers, the historic citadel of Barabati in Cuttack was founded in 1229 CE by King Anangabhima Deva III. Legend recounts that the king, while hunting in the marshland, observed a small hare courageously repelling a royal hawk—an omen that this land possessed unmatched valor. Persian chronicler Shams-i Siraj Afif and Mughal historian Abu’l-Fazl documented that Barabati housed an opulent nine-storey palace (Nava-Tala Prasada) surrounded by stone bastions and a deep moat (Ghai) filled with voracious crocodiles. Though colonial bombardment in 1803 tore down its upper masonry for road metal, the monumental arched gateway, laterite moat, and sacred 32-pillared hall foundations still echo the imperial resonance of Gajapati emperors who ruled from the Ganges to the Godavari.

storyText: When Mahatma Gandhi initiated the Salt March in 1930, the sleepy coastal hamlet of Inchudi in Balasore district emerged as the second most active theater of the Salt Satyagraha in British India. Led by freedom fighter Acharya Harihar Das, a contingent of volunteers marched 240 kilometers from Cuttack’s Swaraj Ashram to Inchudi. On April 14, 1930, defying armed British police cordons, the satyagrahis gathered coastal brine in earthen pots to boil illicit salt. Revered women leaders including Rama Devi, Malati Choudhury, Sarala Devi, and Kokila Devi mobilized thousands of village women who shielded the salt heaps with their bodies. The police unleashed brutal lathi charges, yet thousands queued up daily to court arrest, earning Inchudi the immortal title "Dandi of Eastern India".

translations.or: ୧୯୪୨ ଭାରତ ଛାଡ଼ ଆନ୍ଦୋଳନ ସମୟରେ ଭଦ୍ରକର ଇରମ ମେଳଣ ପଡ଼ିଆରେ ଏକତ୍ରିତ ହୋଇଥିବା ନିରୀହ ଜନତାଙ୍କ ଉପରେ ଇଂରେଜ ପୋଲିସ ଗୁଳିଚାଳନା କରି ୨୯ ଜଣଙ୍କୁ ହତ୍ୟା କରିଥିଲା। ଏହା ରକ୍ତତୀର୍ଥ ନାମରେ ବିଖ୍ୟାତ।
translations.hi: 1942 के भारत छोड़ो आंदोलन के दौरान भद्रक के इरम मैदान में एकत्रित निहत्थे देशभक्तों पर ब्रिटिश पुलिस ने गोलियाँ बरसाईं जिसमें 29 लोग शहीद हुए। इसे ओडिशा का दूसरा जलियांवाला बाग कहा जाता है।

storyText: On September 28, 1942, during the height of the Quit India movement, the coastal enclave of Eram in Bhadrak district became the site of the second largest single civilian massacre in India’s freedom struggle, earning the solemn name "Rakta Tirtha" (The Pilgrimage of Blood). Over five thousand villagers had assembled peacefully on a small field bordered on three sides by the Gamei and Kansbans rivers. Police Deputy Superintendent Kunjabihari Mohanty blocked the sole narrow exit and ordered open rifle fire without issuing a dispersal warning. Within minutes, 29 freedom fighters were killed on the spot and 56 sustained grave bullet wounds, including a heroic woman named Pari Bewa who died cradling the tricolor flag. Their supreme sacrifice broke the colonial stranglehold over coastal Odisha.

translations.or: ପଣ୍ଡିତ ରଘୁନାଥ ମୁର୍ମୁ ୧୯୨୫ ମସିହାରେ ମୟୂରଭଞ୍ଜର ରାଇରଙ୍ଗପୁରରେ ସାନ୍ତାଳୀ ଭାଷା ପାଇଁ ପବିତ୍ର ଅଲ୍ ଚିକି ଲିପି ଉଦ୍ଭାବନ କରି ଆଦିବାସୀ ସଂସ୍କୃତିକୁ ଅମର କରିଥିଲେ।

storyText: Deep inside the dense sal and mahua forests of Mayurbhanj, nestled beneath the misty biosphere peaks of Similipal, lives the Santhal community—guardians of one of the world’s oldest continuous oral cosmologies. According to Santhal lore, the Supreme Creator Marang Buru shaped the earth from cosmic waters with the aid of the crab, the turtle, and the earthworm, breathing life into the ancestral swans Has and Hasil. For centuries, this profound wisdom remained purely oral until visionary scholar Guru Gomke Pandit Raghunath Murmu of Rairangpur invented the indigenous "Ol Chiki" script in 1925. Murmu modeled the 30 phonetic characters directly on the organic geometries of nature: the shape of a bird taking flight, a falling sal leaf, and ancient rock engravings. Today, Ol Chiki is recognized under the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

storyText: Along the shimmering banks of the Mahanadi river in Western Odisha, master weavers of the Meher community practice an intricate mathematical craft known worldwide as Sambalpuri Bandha or double-Ikat. Unlike printed fabrics, the design is mathematically conceived before weaving begins: individual cotton or mulberry silk yarn bundles are tied with waterproof threads and immersed in natural dye vats. The process repeats up to a dozen times to produce traditional motifs—the sacred Shankha (conch), Padma (lotus), and Matsya (fish). Guided by master revivalist Padmashree Krutartha Acharya in the mid-20th century, Sambalpuri handloom evolved into a globally celebrated Geographical Indication (GI) treasure. Wearing a Sambalpuri saree is not merely draped fashion; it is wearing months of hand-tied poetic geometry.

storyText: Every winter in December or January, the commercial town of Bargarh transforms into Mathura, the Jeera river becomes the Yamuna, and the village of Ambapali across the water becomes holy Gopapura. Spanning an astonishing eight square kilometers, Dhanu Yatra is officially certified as the largest open-air theater in the world. For eleven unbroken days, the actor portraying demon King Kansa holds real administrative court: riding an elephant through the streets, issuing humorous decrees to state ministers, imposing playful fines on district collectors, and interrogating civic officials on civic roads and water supply. The entire citizenry becomes the drama’s cast without a single written script. The festival culminates in the dramatic duel where Lord Krishna slays King Kansa, symbolizing the eternal triumph of truth over tyranny.

storyText: Born in the remote tribal hamlet of Tentuliguma in Koraput district, Laxman Nayak was a charismatic Bhumia tribal headman whose profound adherence to Mahatma Gandhi earned him the revered title "Tribal Gandhi". In the dense deciduous forests of the Eastern Ghats, Nayak mobilized indigenous forest dwellers against crushing colonial forest laws, the forced unpaid labor (Bethia) system, and oppressive liquor excise levies. During the 1942 Quit India movement, he led a peaceful march of thousands of unarmed tribal men carrying the tricolor to Matili police station. The colonial authorities opened indiscriminate fire, killed several marchers, and framed Nayak in a fabricated forest guard murder case. On March 29, 1943, Laxman Nayak mounted the gallows in Berhampur jail with a smile, chanting "Vande Mataram" and "Inquilab Zindabad".

storyText: Perched atop the verdant Purnagiri hill overlooking the winding Rushikulya river, the shrine of Maa Tara Tarini is venerated as one of the four ancient Adi Shakti Pithas of India, representing the Stana Pitha (breast relic) of Goddess Sati. The sanctum preserves two revered stone idols carved with gold crowns: Tara and Tarini, twin manifestations of primal feminine energy. For millennia, ancient Odishan sea-merchants (Sadhavas) offered prayers here before setting sail from the nearby ancient port of Palur for Bali, Java, and Sumatra, invoking the goddesses to guide them through monsoon tempests. The Chaitra Yatra festival in spring witnesses hundreds of thousands of pilgrims climbing the 999 stone steps to offer tonsured hair and seek divine protection.

storyText: Lying alongside the sacred Baitarani river, Jajpur was the historic capital Guhasidevapattana of the Bhauma-Kara rulers who governed ancient Kalinga in the 8th and 9th centuries CE. Here stands the ancient temple of Maa Biraja, featuring an exceedingly rare 5th-century Gupta-period two-armed Mahishasuramardini trampling the buffalo demon. Jajpur is also the gateway to the renowned "Diamond Triangle" of Vajrayana Buddhism—Lalitagiri, Ratnagiri, and Udayagiri. During extensive Archaeological Survey of India excavations at Lalitagiri, archaeologists unearthed four nested relic caskets made of Khondalite stone, steatite, silver, and gold holding charred sacred bone relics widely identified with Gautama Buddha or his principal disciples. The monastery ruins reveal carved stone gateways, multi-storeyed dormitories, and an apsidal chaitya hall that drew scholars from across Southeast Asia.

storyText: In the mineral-rich highlands of Kendujhar where the sacred Baitarani river emerges from the rock cleft of Gonasika, indigenous Bhuyan and Juang tribes lived under ancestral sovereignty. In 1891, the feudal King Dhanurjay Bhanja, backed by British political agents, forced thousands of tribal families into brutal uncompensated labor (Bethi) to construct mountain highways. An articulate Bhuyan surveyor trained in Cuttack named Dharanidhar Naik rose as their leader. Naik organized the legendary "Bhuyan Meli": tribal clans surrounded the royal palace, seized colonial armories, and established a parallel indigenous government with Dharanidhar acting as the people’s Dewan. Though British regiments crushed the rebellion with cavalry charges, Naik’s courtroom speeches in Cuttack exposed colonial exploitation to the national press.

storyText: Perched at an elevation of 3,000 feet above sea level in the Eastern Ghats, Daringbadi is affectionately acclaimed as the "Kashmir of Odisha". Named after Daring Sahib, a British forest officer who founded a summer retreat here in the 19th century, the plateau experiences sub-zero winter temperatures with frost settling on pine needles and sprawling organic coffee estates. Surrounding these mist-veiled hills live the Kutia Kondh and Desia Kondh communities, whose organic farming methods yield the prized "Kandhamal Haladi" (turmeric), celebrated globally with a Geographical Indication (GI) tag for its exceptionally high curcumin content and natural aromatic healing qualities.

storyText: In the moonlit early hours of October 11, 1938, along the rain-swollen banks of the Brahmani river at Nilakanthapur ghat in Dhenkanal, occurred one of the most heroic moments in global freedom lore. Baji Rout, an orphaned 12-year-old boatman boy affiliated with the Prajamandal (People’s Movement), was guarding his wooden ferryboat. A troop of heavily armed British police officers, having fired on peaceful demonstrators in Bhuban village, arrived at the ferry ghat fleeing native wrath. The commander ordered Baji to ferry them across. Knowing that crossing would allow them to escape justice, the young boy boldly refused. Enraged, a British soldier struck him with a rifle butt and shot him in the head. Baji Rout died instantly alongside four fellow boatmen, becoming India’s youngest documented freedom martyr and inspiring Sachidananda Routray’s immortal Odia poem "Baji Rout".

storyText: In the mid-20th century, in the quiet heritage bazaar of Nayagarh, a humble confectionery craftsman named Sudarsan Sahu inadvertently created one of India’s most celebrated traditional desserts: Chhena Poda, the roasted cheese cake of Odisha. Having leftover fresh cow-milk cottage cheese (Chhena) at the close of business, Sahu mixed it with raw sugar, semolina, crushed green cardamom, and raisins, wrapped the mixture securely in fresh Sal leaves, and placed it inside his charcoal oven under glowing embers overnight. By morning, the sugar had caramelized into a deep golden-brown crust while retaining a soft, melt-in-the-mouth, aromatic cheese interior. When India’s first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru visited Odisha, he tasted this confection and marveled at its smoky complexity. Today, Nayagarh Chhena Poda is an ambassador of Odia culinary pride.

storyText: Tucked within the dense deciduous forests of Ramagiri hills in Koraput district, Gupteswar—literally "The Hidden Lord"—is a subterranean limestone cave sanctuary dedicated to Lord Shiva. Pilgrims descend through a cool stone cavern to reach a massive natural stalagmite lingam that remains perpetually moist from subterranean mineral drops. Local tribal folklore recounts that the lingam was discovered by a hunter tracking a deer who was astounded to see a cow voluntarily offering milk over the hidden rock. Flowing adjacent to the cave is the sacred Shabari river, forever linked in regional belief with the devoted forest ascetic Shabari who offered sweet berries to Lord Rama during his exile.

storyText: Isolated across the steep hills of Khairput block in Malkangiri district, the Bonda highlanders—referred to as the Remo (The People)—represent one of the most ancient Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) on the Indian subcontinent, linguistically belonging to the Austroasiatic Munda family. Bonda women are instantly recognizable by their striking, culturally codified attire: intricately woven brass rings, massive tiers of multi-colored glass beads covering their torsos, shaved heads crowned with palmyra fillets, and short hand-loomed cloth called Ringa woven on miniature back-strap looms. Every Thursday at the vibrant weekly Onukadelli haat, Bonda families walk down mountain trails to barter organic forest honey, millets, and wild herbs, maintaining social customs that have endured for millennia.

storyText: Rising dramatically between Rayagada and Kalahandi districts, the emerald forested ridge of Niyamgiri is the sacred habitat of the Dongria Kondh. To the Dongria, Niyamgiri is not merely a mountain; it is the physical abode of Niyam Raja, the divine provider of streams, wild tubers, and mountain balance. The Dongria are famed horticulturists who cultivate terraced pineapple, jackfruit, and ginger groves without chemicals. Their artistic soul shines in the iconic "Kapdaganda" shawl—an intricately embroidered white cotton drape stitched by Dongria maidens using triangular green, yellow, and red motifs that represent mountain peaks, clan identity, and solar energy. In 2024, the Kapdaganda shawl was awarded Geographical Indication (GI) status, honoring their living sacred heritage.

title: Nirmal Munda & The Amko Simko Tribal Uprising of 1939

translations.or: ୧୯୩୯ ମସିହାରେ ସୁନ୍ଦରଗଡ଼ର ଆମକୋ ସିମକୋ ମଇଦାନରେ ଇଂରେଜ ସୈନ୍ୟମାନେ ନିର୍ମଳ ମୁଣ୍ଡାଙ୍କ ନେତୃତ୍ୱରେ ଏକତ୍ରିତ ଶତାଧିକ ଆଦିବାସୀଙ୍କ ଉପରେ ଗୁଳି ଚଳାଇ ୪୦ ରୁ ଅଧିକ ଲୋକଙ୍କୁ ହତ୍ୟା କରିଥିଲେ।

storyText: On April 25, 1939, deep in the tribal belt of Gangpur State (modern Sundargarh district), a tragic massacre unfolded at Amko Simko field. Led by Nirmal Munda, a courageous World War I veteran turned peasant leader, thousands of indigenous Munda, Oraon, and Kharia villagers gathered to present a petition resisting exorbitant land taxation and feudal oppression by the Regent Queen Rani Janaki Ratho. Fearing a full-scale tribal insurrection, British Political Agent Lt. E. W. Margerison dispatched troops from the Royal Garhwal Rifles. When Nirmal Munda refused to surrender, troops opened point-blank rifle fire into the crowd. Official reports suppressed casualties, but local oral tradition records that more than 40 tribal patriots perished, making Amko Simko one of the most heroic chapters in tribal anti-colonial resistance.

storyText: Bordered by the vast waters of the Hirakud reservoir, Debrigarh Wildlife Sanctuary is not only a haven for the four-horned antelope (Chousingha), Indian bison (Gaur), and leopards; it is sacred soil steeped in 1857 revolutionary history. When Sambalpur’s legendary leader Veer Surendra Sai escaped from Hazaribagh prison in 1857, he transformed the rugged Barapahad hills of Debrigarh into his guerrilla stronghold. Aided by Gond tribal headmen like Madho Singh and Kamal Singh Dau, Sai established hidden stone bastions inside the dense sal and bamboo ravines. The British military conducted relentless expeditions but failed for years to conquer Debrigarh’s natural mountain forts.

storyText: Where the mighty Mahanadi river carves an astonishing 22-kilometer canyon through the Eastern Ghats, lies Satkosia Gorge—derived from the Odia word "Sat Kosh" meaning seven leagues (approximately 14 miles). Recognized as a UNESCO biosphere habitat, the deep turquoise waters of Tikarpada are home to India’s pioneering freshwater crocodile conservation research project, initiated in 1975 with United Nations FAO support to rescue the critically endangered Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) and Mugger. storyText: Set upon a sprawling granite outcrop in Balangir district, Ranipur Jharial—known anciently as "Soma Tirtha"—is home to one of only four hypaethral (roofless) circular Chausathi Yogini temples surviving in India. Built in the 9th century CE by the Somavamshi kings, the sandstone circular cloister contains 64 carved wall niches enshrining dynamic dancing feminine deities, centered around an elevated sanctum where three-faced Lord Shiva as Nataraja performs the cosmic dance of dissolution and creation. Unlike orthodox walled temples, this open-air circular mandala allowed midnight esoteric Kaula-Kapalika practitioners to channel astral celestial currents under the open starry sky.

storyText: Along the southern bank of the Mahanadi in Boudh district stand three miniature architectural masterpieces: the Rameswar, Siddheswar, and Kapileswar temples, built around the late 9th century CE under the early Bhanja kings. These shrines are internationally renowned among architectural historians for their unique eight-pointed star-shaped ground plan (stellate design). Each projection is carved with exquisite geometric miniature niches, gaja-sinha motifs, and serpentine Naga pillars that catch the morning sunlight at shifting dynamic angles. Nearby at Jagati stands a colossal 7th-century stone Buddha in Bhumisparsha mudra, testifying to the peaceful syncretism of Shaivism and Mahayana Buddhism along the ancient Mahanadi trade corridors.

storyText: Cascading over terraced quartzite cliffs in Deogarh district, the roaring Pradhanpat waterfall fills the forest valley with cooling mountain spray. Yet Deogarh was not only blessed by nature; under the enlightened reign of King Sir Basudev Sudhal Deb of Bamanda (1850-1903), this remote forest principality became the intellectual capital of modern Odia literature. In 1885, the king established the Jagannath Ballav Press—the first high-speed printing press in Western Odisha—and launched the legendary weekly journal "Sambalpur Hitaishini". Scholars, poets, and pioneers like Radhanath Ray, Fakir Mohan Senapati, and Gangadhar Meher gathered at Deogarh palace to ignite a renaissance of the Odia language.

storyText: Soaring 4,925 feet above the azure Bay of Bengal in Gajapati district, Mahendragiri is celebrated in the Ramayana and Mahabharata as the sacred mountain where Parashurama performed intense austerities. Dotted across the mist-shrouded summit are three stone shrines dedicated to Kunti, Yudhisthira, and Bhima, constructed of monumental Cyclopean granite blocks dating to early medieval times. On the slopes below dwell the Lanjia Saora community, renowned creators of "Idital" murals. Dedicated to their ancestor spirits (Labasum), Idital paintings are executed on reddish-brown mud walls using rice paste and natural straw brushes, portraying cosmic trees, dancing hunters, and ceremonial elephants in vibrant geometric silhouettes.

storyText: In the fertile coastal heartland of Jagatsinghpur at Jhankad stands the ancient shrine of Maa Sarala, the presiding deity of wisdom and literature in Odisha. In the 15th century, during the glorious reign of Gajapati Emperor Kapilendra Deva, an unlettered farmer named Siddheswar Parida spent his days plowing paddy fields while chanting prayers to the Mother. According to regional legend, Goddess Sarala appeared in a vision and endowed him with divine eloquence, rechristening him "Sarala Das" (Servant of Sarala). With an iron stylus on dried palm leaves, Sarala Das composed the monumental 18-parva Odia Mahabharata, democratizing the Sanskrit epic into the vibrant colloquial idiom of Odisha’s peasants and soldier-paikas, giving birth to classical Odia literature.

translations.or: ଝାରସୁଗୁଡ଼ାର ବେଲପାହାଡ଼ ଜଙ୍ଗଲରେ ଥିବା ବିକ୍ରମଖୋଲ ଗୁମ୍ଫାରେ ପ୍ରାଗୈତିହାସିକ ମାନବ ଦ୍ୱାରା ଖୋଦିତ ଏକ ରହସ୍ୟମୟ ଲିପି ଆଜି ମଧ୍ୟ ବିଦ୍ୱାନମାନଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ ଏକ ଅସମାହିତ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ ହୋଇ ରହିଛି।

storyText: Hidden within the forested sandstone ridges near Belpahar in Jharsuguda district lies Bikramkhol—a massive natural rock shelter 115 feet long and 30 feet high. In 1930, British archaeologist K. P. Jayaswal documented an astonishing discovery: engraved across the vertical rock face were deep incisions of symbols, geometric signs, and stylized figures painted with red ochre and black iron oxide. The inscription exhibits pictographic and linear forms that scholars have compared to the Indus Valley Script and early Brahmi, sparking vibrant debates across world archaeology. Local Gond communities have protected the shelter for generations as the resting pavilion of ancient celestial ascetics.

storyText: Situated on the bank of the Sandul river in Kalahandi district, the ancient fortified site of Asurgarh represents one of Eastern India’s most significant urban archaeological breakthroughs. Carbon-14 dating of charcoal samples from recent Archaeological Survey of India excavations confirmed human occupation dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 5th century CE. The trapezoidal fortress was protected by a massive mud-and-brick rampart surrounded by a wide defensive moat linked to an ingenious hydraulic reservoir system. Excavators unearthed silver punch-marked coins, terracotta figurines, glass beads, carnelian ornaments, and iron weaponry that establish Asurgarh as a thriving gem-cutting center and international trading post along the ancient Dakshinapatha highway connecting coastal Kalinga to Central India.

storyText: Spanning the estuarine delta of the Brahmani, Baitarani, and Dhamra rivers in Kendrapara district, Bhitarkanika is a pristine 672-square-kilometer mangrove wilderness declared a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance. Interlaced by tidal creeks, Bhitarkanika harbors the world’s highest density of endangered Saltwater Crocodiles (Crocodylus porosus), including record-breaking giants measuring over 20 feet in length documented in the Guinness Book of World Records. Alongside the crocodiles thrive eight species of dazzling kingfishers, spotted deer, wild boars, and the endangered Horseshoe Crab. In monsoon, tens of thousands of migratory birds nest in the Bagagahana heronry, transforming this ancient royal hunting preserve of the Kanika Raja into a thriving ecological sanctuary.

translations.or: ୧୯୪୨ ମସିହା ଅଗଷ୍ଟ ୨୪ରେ ନବରଙ୍ଗପୁରର ପାପଡ଼ାହାଣ୍ଡି ତୁରୀ ନଦୀ ସେତୁ ନିକଟରେ ଇଂରେଜ ପୋଲିସ ନିରୀହ କଂଗ୍ରେସ କର୍ମୀଙ୍କ ଉପରେ ଗୁଳି ଚଳାଇ ୧୫ ଜଣଙ୍କୁ ହତ୍ୟା କରିଥିଲା।
translations.hi: 1942 में नवरंगपुर के पापड़ाहांडी में तुरी नदी के संकरे पुल पर ब्रिटिश पुलिस ने शांतिपूर्ण सत्याग्रहियों पर गोलियाँ बरसाईं जिसमें 15 वीर सपूत शहीद हुए।

storyText: On August 24, 1942, during the nationwide Quit India movement, the wooden bridge spanning the swollen Turi river at Papadahandi in Nabarangpur district became a battleground of freedom. Inspired by Mahatma Gandhi’s call to "Do or Die", thousands of unarmed peasant and tribal men from surrounding villages marched peacefully toward the Dabugam police outpost. As the procession reached the middle of the narrow bridge, a detachment of armed British police blocked both ends of the bridge, trapping the satyagrahis over deep turbulent waters. Without warning, the inspector ordered open firing. Fifteen brave patriots were killed by bullets on the bridge while dozens jumped into the floodwaters and drowned. Over a hundred were gravely wounded. Today, the majestic Shahid Stambha memorial stands beside the river, where thousands gather every August 24 to honor their eternal sacrifice.

storyText: Cradled in the Sunabeda plateau of Nuapada district, the Maraguda valley is an extraordinary archaeological treasure house. Excavations by the Odisha State Archaeology department revealed brick foundations of an extensive 5th-century CE fortified urban settlement, Buddhist monasteries with Chaitya halls, and a remarkable temple complex dedicated to Goddess Mahishasuramardini. Historians correlate this site with Sharabhapura, the legendary lost capital of the Sharabhapuriya kings. Nearby at Patalganga, a perennial natural hot spring bubbles crystal-clear mineral water out of granite boulders, where pilgrims take holy baths on solar eclipses and Sankranti to wash away illnesses.

storyText: Lovingly celebrated as the "Second Varanasi of Odisha", Subarnapur sits serenely at the sacred confluence of the Mahanadi and Tel rivers. The town is famous for the revered shrine of Maa Lankeswari, perched dramatically atop a dark granite boulder in the middle of the river, where boatmen make offerings before navigating turbulent monsoon rapids. Subarnapur is also the legendary home of Sonepuri Bomkai (Sonepur Bandha)—an internationally celebrated Geographical Indication (GI) handloom weave. Master weavers use jala extra-weft techniques on traditional pit looms to craft sarees adorned with ancient tribal motifs such as the bitter gourd (Karela phula), peacock, and temple spires.
